# 1 Maccabees — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous pro-Hasmonean writer, likely a court historian |
| **Date** | c. 100 BCE (covering events 175–134 BCE) |
| **Audience** | Jewish readers under Hasmonean rule; a defense of dynastic legitimacy |
| **Genre** | Historical narrative, deliberately imitating Samuel–Kings |
| **Timeline** | From Antiochus IV's accession (175 BCE) through Simon's assassination (134 BCE) |
| **In One Sentence** | The story of how one priestly family saved Judaism from annihilation — told with the austere dignity of Scripture itself. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

To understand 1 Maccabees, you must understand what Alexander the Great's conquests actually did to the ancient world. When Alexander died in 323 BCE, his generals carved his empire into successor kingdoms. Palestine fell between two of them: the Ptolemies of Egypt to the south and the Seleucids of Syria to the north. For over a century, these empires competed for control of Judea, but life under Hellenistic rule was, for many Jews, tolerable. Greek became the language of commerce, culture, and prestige. Many Jews embraced it willingly.

But by 175 BCE something had changed. Antiochus IV Epiphanes — the "God Manifest," as he styled himself — came to the Seleucid throne with debts, ambitions, and an ideological agenda. He saw cultural unity as a political necessity and moved to accelerate the Hellenization of Judea with a force that crossed from cultural pressure into religious persecution. The Jerusalem Temple was rededicated to Zeus. The Torah was outlawed. Circumcision became a capital offense. Sabbath observance was punishable by death. The "abomination of desolation" — an altar to Zeus erected over the Temple altar — became the defining outrage of the age. For a people whose entire identity was bound to Torah, this was not merely oppression. It was an existential attack on the covenant itself.

Into this crisis stepped Mattathias, an elderly priest from Modein, and his five sons. What began as a single act of violent refusal — Mattathias killing a Jew who was about to offer a pagan sacrifice — became a guerrilla war, then a full insurrection, then a dynasty. The book of 1 Maccabees is that dynasty's official account of its own legitimacy. It is simultaneously a military chronicle, a theological argument, and a piece of political literature — all written in a Hebrew that its author shaped to echo the cadences of Samuel and Kings, as if to say: this family belongs in the same story as David.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The author of 1 Maccabees had a specific political purpose that shapes every sentence. By the time of writing (c. 100 BCE), the Hasmonean family had secured not only military victory but also the high priesthood and, eventually, kingship itself. This was deeply controversial. The Hasmoneans were priests, not Davidides; their assumption of royal power violated the traditional separation of priestly and kingly lines. Competing Jewish groups — the Pharisees, the Essenes who gave us the Dead Sea Scrolls, priestly conservatives — questioned their legitimacy.

The book answers these critics through narrative. It presents Mattathias and his sons as the only possible heroes, the people through whom God's purposes moved — not via miracles, which are conspicuously absent, but through human courage, military genius, and faithful Torah observance. Simon's chapter (14) in particular reads like a legitimation document, with the people formally ratifying Hasmonean rule in language that echoes covenant ratification ceremonies. The author is not neutral. He is writing the Hasmonean version of events for a Hasmonean audience, and the book should be read with that agenda in full view.

Yet the author's partisanship does not make the book unreliable as history — quite the opposite. His proximity to events, his access to official records, his concern for precise dates and treaty texts, all make 1 Maccabees the most historically credible source we have for this period. Scholars who must choose between 1 and 2 Maccabees for a historical fact almost always prefer 1 Maccabees. It reads like a man who has seen the documents and talked to survivors, and who wants, above all, to get the record straight — even as he frames that record in the most favorable possible light.

---

## How to Read This Book

Read 1 Maccabees as you would read Samuel or Kings — slowly, attending to the rhythm of battle reports and speeches and laments. The author has crafted this rhythm deliberately. Victories are celebrated; defeats are mourned. Heroes give dying speeches. The land itself is described as defiled and then restored. If you know the Deuteronomistic History, you will feel the echoes constantly: this is their Judges and their David, retold for a new age.

Pay close attention to the four main figures: Mattathias (chapters 1–2), Judas (3–9:22), Jonathan (9:23–12), and Simon (13–16). Each brother inherits a more complex situation than his predecessor. Mattathias ignites the revolt and establishes its principles. Judas wins the impossible battles and rededicated the Temple — the founding miracle of Hanukkah (4:52–59), described here without supernatural language as a feat of engineering and religious restoration. Jonathan shifts from guerrilla warfare to diplomacy, playing Seleucid factions against each other with remarkable skill. Simon achieves what none of his brothers could: political independence, a formal treaty with Rome, and acknowledged sovereignty.

The Roman alliance (chapters 8, 12, 14–15) deserves special attention. To the author, Rome is an admirable world power and a useful counterweight to the Seleucids. He describes Roman governance with something close to admiration. Later history would reveal how catastrophically misguided this alliance was — Rome would eventually swallow Judea whole — but the author writes before that outcome, and his enthusiasm for Rome is genuine. It also tells us something about his political theology: he does not expect God to solve problems miraculously. He expects God's people to form alliances, negotiate treaties, and fight battles.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The most important connection is structural: 1 Maccabees consciously models itself on the Former Prophets. Mattathias's deathbed speech (2:49–70) is a compressed recitation of biblical heroes — Abraham, Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, David, Elijah, Daniel — positioning his sons as the next chapter in that story. The echo of Phinehas is especially significant: just as Phinehas earned an eternal covenant of priesthood by his violent zeal (Numbers 25), Mattathias's violent act at Modein restores that same covenant. The author is making a legal and theological argument, not just a narrative one.

The Hanukkah narrative (4:36–59) connects directly to the dedication of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8) and to Ezra's restoration of worship after the exile. The pattern is: defilement, lamentation, purification, rededication, celebration. The author wants readers to feel this as the third great restoration of Israelite worship.

The alliance texts and diplomatic letters embedded throughout (chapters 8, 12, 14–15) connect to ancient Near Eastern treaty literature and to the covenant documents of the Hebrew Bible. The author uses this genre deliberately, presenting the Hasmoneans as treaty partners of nations — a form of international legitimacy.

Looking forward, 1 Maccabees becomes essential background for the New Testament. The Hasmonean period created the Pharisees, the Sadducees, and the conditions that eventually produced the Herodian dynasty. John the Baptist and Jesus both operate within a Jewish world still processing the trauma and legacy of the Maccabean revolt. The phrase "abomination of desolation" (1:54), cited by Daniel (9:27, 11:31, 12:11) and quoted by Jesus in Mark 13:14, passes through this book.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The silence about God is the loudest thing in this book. Unlike almost every other biblical narrative, 1 Maccabees contains no miracles, no divine speech, no angel appearances, and no direct statement that "the LORD was with" any of its heroes. God is mentioned — in prayers, in laments, in the phrase "Heaven" used as a circumlocution — but God does not act visibly. This was noticed in antiquity and has been debated ever since. Some scholars see it as the author's theological realism: God works through human agents, and faith is demonstrated by what you are willing to do, not by what you expect God to do for you. Others see the absence as reflecting a crisis of faith — how could God have allowed the Temple's defilement? Either way, the silence is not accidental. It is the book's most provocative theological move.

The social world of apostasy is also easy to miss. The book treats Jews who cooperated with Hellenization as villains, but their motivations were complex. Many "Hellenizers" were educated, cosmopolitan priests and aristocrats who genuinely believed that cultural accommodation was the path to survival and prosperity. The Torah-loyal resistance was not the only rational response to the Seleucid crisis; it was one response among several, and it won — which is why we are reading about it. The "wicked men" of chapter 1 were real people making real choices in a genuinely ambiguous situation.

The book also embeds authentic primary documents — letters, decrees, treaty texts — that are invaluable for historians. The Spartan correspondence (12:5–23) and the Roman senatus consultum (8:23–32) are debated for authenticity but preserve real diplomatic texture from the period. When you read these documents, you are looking at something as close to archival evidence as the ancient world provides.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

1 Maccabees survives only in Greek, though it was originally written in Hebrew — a Hebrew original that Jerome mentions having seen but which has not survived. This paradox has shaped its canonical fate. It was never included in the Hebrew Bible (the Tanakh), which was essentially fixed by the rabbinic councils of the late first and second centuries CE. The rabbis who shaped that canon were working in the aftermath of the catastrophic Roman destruction of the Temple (70 CE) and the Bar Kokhba revolt (135 CE). The Hasmonean dynasty, which 1 Maccabees celebrates, had ended in Roman conquest and the very disasters the rabbis were now living through. Celebrating Hasmonean military prowess was not the spirituality they were building.

The Greek-speaking Jewish community, whose Scriptures were the Septuagint (LXX), included 1 Maccabees — which is how it reached the early Christian churches. Because the early church inherited the Septuagint, 1 Maccabees became part of Christian Old Testament collections. The Catholic and Orthodox traditions have retained it as deuterocanonical — "second canon," meaning authoritative Scripture of a slightly different status. The Protestant Reformers, following their principle of returning to the Hebrew Scriptures (sola scriptura operating against the Vulgate tradition), excluded it along with the other deuterocanonicals. Protestant Bibles today do not include it, though many historically included it in an Apocrypha section.

This means that billions of people who celebrate Hanukkah lights or hear references to the "Maccabees" in Christian liturgy are drawing on a book they have never read, from a tradition that technically no longer considers it Scripture.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 336–323 BCE | Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Empire |
| 323 BCE | Death of Alexander; empire divided among generals |
| 198 BCE | Seleucids take Palestine from the Ptolemies |
| 175 BCE | Antiochus IV Epiphanes becomes Seleucid king |
| 167 BCE | Desecration of the Temple; Torah outlawed |
| 166 BCE | Mattathias's revolt begins at Modein |
| 165/4 BCE | Judas Maccabeus rededication of Temple — Hanukkah |
| 160 BCE | Judas killed at the battle of Elasa |
| 152 BCE | Jonathan becomes High Priest |
| 143 BCE | Jonathan captured and killed by Trypho |
| 142 BCE | Simon achieves political independence from the Seleucids |
| 134 BCE | Simon assassinated by his son-in-law Ptolemy |
